p.src: Now after Lu Xun of Eastern Wu had driven back the Wei army, the King of Wu appointed him General Who Supports the State and Marquis of Jiangling, and placed him in charge of Jingzhou as its governor; from then on, all military authority rested with Lu Xun. Zhang Zhao and Gu Yong memorialized the King of Wu, requesting that he inaugurate an era name of his own. Sun Quan agreed and accordingly proclaimed the first year of Huangwu. Suddenly word came that the ruler of Wei had sent an envoy, and Sun Quan summoned him in. The envoy was instructed to explain: “Earlier, Shu sent men to make a request of Wei. Wei failed for a time to discern the truth and therefore raised troops in response; now Wei deeply regrets it and intends to send four armies to seize Sichuan. Eastern Wu may come and support us. If we gain the lands of Shu, we shall divide them equally between us.” Hearing this, Sun Quan could not decide and therefore consulted Zhang Zhao, Gu Yong, and the others. Zhang Zhao said, “Lu Boyan possesses extraordinary insight. You may ask him.” Sun Quan at once summoned Lu Xun. When Lu Xun arrived, he submitted: “Cao Pi holds the Central Plains firmly, and we cannot act hastily against him; yet if we refuse him now, he will surely become our enemy. In my judgment, neither Wei nor Wu has anyone capable of matching Zhuge Liang. For now, reluctantly consent, ready the army, and merely observe how the four armies fare. If those four armies prevail and Sichuan is imperiled, leaving Zhuge Liang unable to succor both front and rear, Your Majesty should then send troops in support and seize Chengdu first. This is the best plan; if the four armies are defeated, we can deliberate anew.” Sun Quan followed his counsel and told the Wei envoy, “Our military supplies are not yet prepared. Once a day has been chosen, our forces shall set out.” The envoy bowed farewell and departed.

p.src: Sun Quan sent men to investigate and learned that the western tribes had marched out through Xiping Pass, but upon seeing Ma Chao had withdrawn without a fight; Meng Huo of the Southern Man had raised troops to attack the four commanderies, but Wei Yan routed them all with a feigned-force stratagem, driving them back to their caves; Meng Da’s army from Shangyong had fallen ill halfway and could proceed no farther; and when Cao Zhen’s forces emerged through Yangping Pass, Zhao Zilong barred every strategic defile—truly, one general guarded the pass, and ten thousand men could not break through. Cao Zhen encamped in the Xie Valley road, but returned without gaining a victory. When Sun Quan learned these tidings, he said to his civil and military officers, “Lu Boyan’s foresight is truly divine. Had I acted recklessly, I would have made an enemy of Western Shu as well.” Suddenly it was reported that Western Shu had sent Deng Zhi. Zhang Zhao said, “This too is one of Zhuge Liang’s schemes to turn back an army. He has sent Deng Zhi as a persuader.” Sun Quan asked, “How should I answer him?” Zhang Zhao replied, “First set a great cauldron before the hall, fill it with several hundred catties of oil, and heat it from below with charcoal. When the oil boils, choose a thousand tall, broad-faced warriors, each holding a sword, and line them up from the palace gate to the hall; then summon Deng Zhi to your presence. Do not wait for him to begin his persuasive speech. Charge him with repeating Li Yiji’s attempt to persuade Qi and, following that precedent, boil him alive. Then we shall see how he answers.”

p.src: Sun Quan followed his advice, set up the oil cauldron, ordered warriors to stand on either side with weapons in hand, and summoned Deng Zhi. Deng Zhi straightened his robes and cap and entered. Upon reaching the palace gate, he saw two ranks of fearsome warriors, each bearing a steel sword, great axe, long blade, or short halberd, lined all the way to the front of the hall. Deng Zhi understood their intent, but showed no fear and strode proudly onward. Before the hall he also saw the oil seething in the cauldron. The warriors on either side watched him closely, but Deng Zhi merely smiled faintly. A close attendant led him before the curtain, where Deng Zhi made a deep bow without kneeling. Sun Quan ordered the beaded curtain raised and shouted, “Why do you not bow?” Deng Zhi answered proudly, “An envoy of a superior state does not bow to the ruler of a petty realm.” Sun Quan was furious. “You do not know your own measure! Do you mean to wag your three-inch tongue and imitate Master Li in persuading Qi? Into the oil cauldron with you at once!” Deng Zhi laughed loudly. “Everyone says Eastern Wu abounds in worthy men. Who would have thought it feared a lone scholar!” Sun Quan’s anger sharpened. “Why should I fear a mere fellow like you?” Deng Zhi said, “If you do not fear Deng Bomiao, why be anxious that I have come to persuade you?” Sun Quan said, “You mean to serve as Zhuge Liang’s persuader and induce me to break with Wei and side with Shu—is that not so?” Deng Zhi replied, “I am but a scholar of Shu and have come especially to discuss what profits or harms the state of Wu. Yet you array soldiers and set out a cauldron to repel a single envoy. How can your capacity be so narrow that it admits nothing?”

p.src: Hearing this, Sun Quan felt alarmed and ashamed. He immediately ordered the warriors away, invited Deng Zhi into the hall, gave him a seat, and asked, “Where do the interests and perils of Wu and Wei lie? I beg you, sir, to instruct me.” Deng Zhi said, “Does Your Majesty wish to make peace with Shu, or with Wei?” Sun Quan said: “I truly wish to make peace with the ruler of Shu; I fear only that the ruler of Shu is young and inexperienced and cannot remain faithful from beginning to end.” Deng Zhi replied, “Your Majesty is a hero destined for this age, and Zhuge Liang is likewise an outstanding genius of his time; Shu has the defenses of its mountains and rivers, while Wu has the fastness of its Three Rivers. If the two states unite as close as lips and teeth, then advancing, they may together swallow the realm; retreating, they may stand as one leg of a tripartite balance. If Your Majesty now presents gifts and professes vassalage to Wei, Wei will surely expect Your Majesty to attend its court and demand that the crown prince serve within its palace; if you refuse, it will raise an army to attack, while Shu too will advance downstream to seize your lands. Then the country south of the Yangtze will no longer belong to Your Majesty. If Your Majesty considers my humble words mistaken, I shall die here before you and forever put an end to my reputation as a persuader.” Having said this, he gathered up his robe, descended from the hall, and made to leap straight into the oil cauldron. Sun Quan hurriedly ordered him stopped, invited him into the rear hall, and treated him with the courtesies accorded an honored guest. Sun Quan said, “Your words, sir, accord precisely with my own intent. I now wish to ally with the ruler of Shu. Would you be willing to act as intermediary for me?” Deng Zhi replied, “The one who wished just now to boil your humble servant was Your Majesty; the one who now wishes to employ your humble servant is also Your Majesty. If Your Majesty is still wavering and undecided, how can you win another’s trust?” Sun Quan said, “My mind is settled. Doubt me no more, sir.”

p.src: The King of Wu then asked Deng Zhi to remain and assembled his officials. “I rule the eighty-one prefectures south of the Yangtze and possess the lands of Jing and Chu besides, yet can it be that we are inferior to the remote region of Western Shu? Shu has Deng Zhi, who has brought no disgrace upon his lord; yet Wu has not a single man who can enter Shu and convey my intentions.” Suddenly one man stepped from the ranks and memorialized, “I am willing to serve as envoy.” All looked and saw a native of Wu in Wu Commandery: his surname was Zhang, his personal name Wen, and his style Huishu; he currently held the post of General of the Gentlemen of the Household. Sun Quan said, “I fear that when you reach Shu and meet Zhuge Liang, you will be unable to convey my true sentiments.” Zhang Wen replied, “Kongming is only a man. Why should I fear him?” Sun Quan was delighted. He rewarded Zhang Wen richly and sent him with Deng Zhi into Sichuan to establish friendly relations.

p.src: Now after Deng Zhi had departed, Kongming memorialized to the Latter Emperor, “Deng Zhi’s mission will certainly succeed. The land of Wu abounds in worthy men; someone will surely come to return the courtesy. Your Majesty should receive him courteously and send him back to Wu, thereby establishing an alliance of friendship. If Wu enters into peace with us, Wei will surely not dare send troops against Shu. Once Wu and Wei are quiet, I shall campaign in the south and pacify the Man regions, and only then turn my designs against Wei. When Wei has been weakened, Eastern Wu too will be unable to endure for long, and the foundations of a reunited empire may be restored.” The Latter Emperor approved.

p.src: Suddenly it was reported that Eastern Wu had sent Zhang Wen with Deng Zhi into Sichuan to return the courtesy. The Latter Emperor assembled his civil and military officers at the vermilion steps and ordered Deng Zhi and Zhang Wen to enter. Zhang Wen, believing himself triumphant, strode proudly into the hall and paid his respects to the Latter Emperor. The Latter Emperor bestowed a brocade-covered seat upon him, seated him to the left of the hall, and held an imperial banquet in his honor. The Latter Emperor did no more than treat him with honor and courtesy. When the banquet ended, the officials escorted Zhang Wen to his lodgings. The next day, Kongming prepared a banquet to entertain him. Kongming said to Zhang Wen, “While the Former Emperor lived, relations with Wu were unfriendly; now he has passed away. Our present sovereign deeply admires the King of Wu and wishes to cast aside old resentments, establish a lasting alliance of friendship, and join forces to defeat Wei. I trust, sir, that you will report this favorably upon your return.” Zhang Wen accepted the charge. When the wine had reached its height, Zhang Wen smiled and laughed with perfect ease, showing a considerable air of arrogance.

p.src: The next day, the Later Emperor presented Zhang Wen with gold and silk, held a banquet at the post pavilion south of the city, and ordered the officials to see him off. Kongming courteously pressed wine upon him. While they were drinking, a man suddenly entered in his cups, gave a proud bow with clasped hands, and took a seat at the banquet. Surprised, Wen asked Kongming, “Who is this man?” Kongming replied, “His surname is Qin, his given name is Mi, and his courtesy name is Zichi. He presently serves as a scholar of Yizhou.” Wen laughed. “You bear the title of scholar, but I wonder whether you have ever truly studied anything?” Mi answered gravely, “Even three-foot children in Shu attend to their studies—how much more would I?” Wen said, “Then tell me what you have studied.” Mi replied, “From astronomy above to geography below, from the Three Teachings and Nine Schools to all the masters and hundred schools, there is nothing I do not comprehend. The rise and fall of ages past and present, and the classics and commentaries of sages and worthies—there is nothing I have not read.” Wen laughed. “Since you make so bold a claim, allow me to question you about Heaven. Does Heaven have a head?” Mi said, “It does.” Wen asked, “In which direction is its head?” Mi replied, “In the west. The Book of Odes says, ‘Then He turned His gaze westward.’ From this we may infer that its head lies in the west.” Wen asked again, “Does Heaven have ears?” Mi replied, “Heaven dwells on high yet hears those below. The Book of Odes says, ‘The crane cries in the distant marsh, and its voice is heard in Heaven.’ Without ears, how could it hear?” Wen asked again, “Does Heaven have feet?” Mi said, “It has feet. The Book of Odes says, ‘Heaven’s steps are fraught with hardship.’ Without feet, how could it walk?” Wen asked again, “Does Heaven have a surname?” Mi said, “How could it have none!” Wen asked, “What surname?” Mi replied, “Liu.” Wen asked, “How do you know?” Mi said, “The Son of Heaven bears the surname Liu; that is how I know.” Wen asked once more, “Is the sun born in the east?” Mi replied, “Though born in the east, it dies in the west.”

p.src: Throughout this exchange, Qin Mi spoke clearly and answered every question without pause, astonishing everyone present. Zhang Wen was left speechless. Mi then asked, “Sir, you are a celebrated scholar of Eastern Wu. Since you questioned me about Heaven, you must surely possess a profound understanding of its principles. In ancient times, when primordial chaos divided, yin and yang were separated. What was light and pure floated upward and became Heaven, while what was heavy and turbid settled below and became Earth. Then Gonggong, defeated in battle, struck Mount Buzhou with his head, breaking the pillar of Heaven and severing the bonds of Earth. Heaven tilted toward the northwest, and Earth sank toward the southeast. Since Heaven was light and pure and floated upward, how could its northwest have tilted? Nor do I know what may exist beyond that which is light and pure. I beg you to instruct me.” Zhang Wen had no answer. Leaving his place, he apologized: “I never imagined that Shu produced so many men of outstanding talent! Hearing this discourse has suddenly cleared away the obstruction from my mind.” Fearing that Wen would be ashamed, Kongming soothed him with kind words: “The questions and challenges exchanged at the banquet were all merely playful talk. You possess a profound knowledge of the way to pacify and govern a realm; why concern yourself with mere verbal sport?” Wen bowed in thanks. Kongming also ordered Deng Zhi to go to Wu and return its courtesy, traveling together with Zhang Wen. Zhang Wen and Deng Zhi took leave of Kongming with bows and set out for Eastern Wu.

p.src: Meanwhile, when the King of Wu saw that Zhang Wen had not yet returned from Shu, he assembled his civil and military officers for consultation. Suddenly, a court attendant reported, “Shu has sent Deng Zhi into our realm with Zhang Wen to return our courtesy.” Quan summoned them inside. Zhang Wen bowed before the hall and gave a full account of the virtues of the Later Emperor and Kongming, saying that they wished to forge an enduring alliance and had specially sent Secretary Deng to return the courtesy. Quan was delighted and held a banquet in Deng Zhi’s honor. Quan asked Deng Zhi, “If Wu and Shu unite in purpose to destroy Wei and bring peace to the realm, would it not be a joy for our two lords to divide it and govern separately?” Zhi replied, “‘There are not two suns in Heaven, nor two kings among the people.’ Should Wei be destroyed, we cannot yet know upon whom Heaven’s Mandate will fall. Those who rule need only cultivate their virtue, and those who serve need only exhaust their loyalty; only then will warfare cease.” Quan laughed heartily. “So frank and sincere are you!” He then bestowed generous gifts upon Deng Zhi and sent him back to Shu. From that time onward, Wu and Shu maintained friendly relations.

p.src: Meanwhile, Wei spies learned of this and reported it with all speed to the Central Plains. When Cao Pi, ruler of Wei, heard the news, he raged, “Wu and Shu have allied; they surely intend to move against the Central Plains. It would be better for Us to attack first.” He therefore assembled all his civil and military officers to discuss raising an army against Wu. By this time, Grand Marshal Cao Ren and Grand Commandant Jia Xu had already died. Attendant-in-Ordinary Xin Pi stepped forward and memorialized, “The Central Plains are vast, but their people are sparse; I see no advantage in resorting to arms. The best plan today is to nurture the troops and establish military farms for ten years, securing ample grain and soldiers. If we employ them afterward, then Wu and Shu may be defeated.” Pi angrily replied, “That is the argument of a pedantic scholar! Now that Wu and Shu are allied, sooner or later they will invade our borders. How can we spare the time to wait ten years?” He immediately issued an edict to raise an army against Wu. Sima Yi memorialized, “Wu is defended by the natural barrier of the Long River, which cannot be crossed without ships. If Your Majesty is resolved to lead the campaign in person, select warships large and small, enter the Huai by way of the Cai and Ying rivers, take Shouchun, proceed to Guangling, cross the river mouth, and advance directly upon Southern Xu. This is the best strategy.” Pi followed his advice. Thereupon, working day and night, they built ten dragon ships, each more than twenty zhang long and capable of carrying over two thousand men. They also prepared more than three thousand warships. In the eighth month of autumn, the fifth year of Huangchu in Wei, officers and soldiers of every rank assembled. Cao Zhen was appointed commander of the vanguard; Zhang Liao, Zhang He, Wen Ping, Xu Huang, and others were made generals to advance first; Xu Chu and Lü Qian guarded the central army; Cao Xiu commanded the rear; and Liu Ye and Jiang Ji served as advisers. The land and naval forces, front and rear, numbered over three hundred thousand, and they set a date to march. Sima Yi was appointed Deputy Director of the Imperial Secretariat and left behind in Xuchang. All major affairs of state were entrusted to Yi’s decision.

u.src: Meanwhile, Wei spies learned of this and reported it with all speed to the Central Plains.
When Cao Pi, ruler of Wei, heard the news, he raged, “Wu and Shu have allied; they surely intend to move against the Central Plains.
It would be better for Us to attack first.”
He therefore assembled all his civil and military officers to discuss raising an army against Wu.
By this time, Grand Marshal Cao Ren and Grand Commandant Jia Xu had already died.
Attendant-in-Ordinary Xin Pi stepped forward and memorialized, “The Central Plains are vast, but their people are sparse; I see no advantage in resorting to arms.
The best plan today is to nurture the troops and establish military farms for ten years, securing ample grain and soldiers. If we employ them afterward, then Wu and Shu may be defeated.”
Pi angrily replied, “That is the argument of a pedantic scholar!
Now that Wu and Shu are allied, sooner or later they will invade our borders. How can we spare the time to wait ten years?”
He immediately issued an edict to raise an army against Wu.
Sima Yi memorialized, “Wu is defended by the natural barrier of the Long River, which cannot be crossed without ships.

If Your Majesty is resolved to lead the campaign in person, select warships large and small, enter the Huai by way of the Cai and Ying rivers, take Shouchun, proceed to Guangling, cross the river mouth, and advance directly upon Southern Xu. This is the best strategy.”
Pi followed his advice.
Thereupon, working day and night, they built ten dragon ships, each more than twenty zhang long and capable of carrying over two thousand men.

p.src: We leave the Wei army setting out. Meanwhile, spies from Eastern Wu learned of the matter and reported it to Wu. A court attendant hurriedly reported to the King of Wu, “Cao Pi, King of Wei, is personally riding aboard a dragon ship and leading over three hundred thousand naval and land troops. They are entering the Huai from the Cai and Ying rivers, assuredly intending to take Guangling, cross the Long River, and descend upon Jiangnan. The danger is grave.” Sun Quan was greatly alarmed and at once assembled his civil and military officers for consultation. Gu Yong said, “Now that Your Highness has allied with Western Shu, you may write to Zhuge Kongming and have him raise an army from Hanzhong, thereby dividing Wei’s strength. At the same time, dispatch a great general to station troops at Southern Xu and resist them.” Quan said, “None but Lu Boyan can bear this grave responsibility.” Yong said, “Lu Boyan is guarding Jingzhou and cannot be moved lightly.” Quan said, “It is not that I do not know this, but at present there is no one capable of taking his place.” Before he had finished, a man stepped from the ranks and declared, “Though I lack ability, I am willing to command an army against the forces of Wei. If Cao Pi personally crosses the Great River, I shall capture him alive and present him to Your Highness. If he does not cross, I shall still slay more than half his troops and make the soldiers of Wei never again dare look Eastern Wu in the face.” Quan looked and saw that it was Xu Sheng. Quan was delighted. “If I have you to defend the region of Jiangnan, what cause have I for worry?” He therefore appointed Xu Sheng General Who Pacifies the East and placed him in overall command of the troops at Jianye and Southern Xu. Sheng thanked him for the favor, accepted the command, and withdrew. He immediately issued orders for the officers and troops to prepare plentiful equipment and raise many banners, as part of his plan to defend the riverbank.

p.src: Suddenly, one man stepped forward and said, “Today, the King has entrusted you with this grave responsibility, hoping that you will defeat the Wei army and capture Cao Pi. Why do you not dispatch the troops at once, cross the river, and meet the enemy in Huainan? If you wait until Cao Pi’s forces arrive, I fear it will be too late.” Xu Sheng looked at him and saw that it was Sun Shao, a nephew of the King of Wu. Sun Shao, whose courtesy name was Gongli, held the rank of General Who Displays Might and had once defended Guangling. He was young and high-spirited, with exceptional courage and daring. Xu Sheng said, “Cao Pi’s forces are powerful, and he has renowned generals leading his vanguard. We must not cross the river to meet him. Once all his ships have gathered along the northern bank, I shall have a plan to defeat him.” Sun Shao said, “I have three thousand troops under my command and know the roads and terrain around Guangling intimately. I wish to go north of the river myself and fight Cao Pi to the death. If I do not prevail, I shall willingly suffer the penalty prescribed by military law.” Xu Sheng refused. Sun Shao stubbornly insisted on going. Xu Sheng remained adamant, while Sun Shao repeatedly demanded leave to depart. Xu Sheng said angrily, “If you disobey my commands in this fashion, how can I possibly control the other generals?” He ordered the guards to drag Sun Shao out and behead him. The executioners escorted Sun Shao beyond the camp gate and raised the black execution banner. One of Sun Shao’s officers hurried to report the matter to Sun Quan. When Sun Quan heard, he swiftly mounted his horse and rode to the rescue. Just as the guards were about to carry out the sentence, Sun Quan arrived. He shouted the executioners away and rescued Sun Shao, who tearfully reported, “In former years I was stationed at Guangling and came to know its terrain intimately. If we do not fight Cao Pi there, but wait until he has descended upon the Yangtze, Eastern Wu will soon be finished!”

p.src: Sun Quan went straight into the camp. Xu Sheng received him and led him into the command tent, where he reported, “Your Majesty appointed me commander-in-chief and charged me with leading the army against Wei. Now Sun Shao, General Who Displays Might, has defied military law and disobeyed orders, an offense punishable by death. Why, Your Majesty, did you pardon him?” Sun Quan replied, “Shao, carried away by youthful vigor, violated military law in error. I earnestly beg you to forgive him.” Xu Sheng said, “The law was established neither by me nor by Your Majesty; it is the statutory punishment of the state. If kinship exempts him, how am I to command the host?” Sun Quan said, “Shao broke the law and should by rights be left to the general’s judgment. Yet though the young man was originally surnamed Yu, my elder brother greatly cherished him and bestowed upon him the surname Sun. He has also rendered me considerable service. If I let him be killed now, I shall betray the duty I owe my brother.” Xu Sheng said, “Out of regard for Your Majesty, I shall suspend his death sentence.” Sun Quan ordered Sun Shao to bow and express his thanks. Sun Shao refused to bow and declared sternly, “As I see it, the only sound course is to lead the army out and defeat Cao Pi! Even if I die, I shall never accept your judgment!” Xu Sheng’s expression changed. Sun Quan rebuked Sun Shao and sent him away, then said to Xu Sheng, “Even without this young man, what loss would Wu suffer? Do not employ him again.” With that, he returned. That night, a man reported to Xu Sheng that Sun Shao had secretly crossed the river with three thousand elite troops from his own command. Fearing that some mishap might occur and leave him unable to face the King of Wu, Xu Sheng summoned Ding Feng, entrusted him with a secret plan, and sent him across the river with three thousand troops to provide support.

p.src: Now the King of Wei sailed his dragon barge to Guangling, where Cao Zhen, commanding the vanguard, had already drawn up his troops along the bank of the great river. Cao Pi asked, “How many troops are there on the opposite bank?” Cao Zhen replied, “Looking across from this distance, we cannot see a single man, nor any banners or encampments.” Cao Pi said, “This must be a ruse. I shall go and examine the true state of affairs myself.” Thereupon, the river passage was cleared, and the dragon barge proceeded directly onto the great river and moored by its bank. The vessel flew five-colored banners adorned with dragons, phoenixes, the sun, and the moon; surrounded by the imperial regalia, it shone with dazzling brilliance. Seated erect within the barge, Cao Pi gazed toward the southern bank but saw not a soul. Turning to Liu Ye and Jiang Ji, he asked, “Can we cross the river?” Liu Ye replied, “In the art of war, the real may appear real or false, and the false real or false. Seeing our great army approach, how could they have made no preparations? Your Majesty must not act rashly. Let us wait three or five days and observe their movements; then we may send the vanguard across to reconnoiter.” Cao Pi said, “Your counsel accords perfectly with my own thoughts.”

p.src: As evening fell that day, they spent the night upon the river. The night was moonless. Every soldier held a lamp or torch, illuminating heaven and earth as brightly as day. Yet when they gazed toward the southern bank, not the faintest glimmer of fire could be seen. Cao Pi asked those about him, “What is the reason for this?” A close attendant replied, “They must have heard that Your Majesty’s heavenly host was approaching and fled at the mere rumor of its coming.” Cao Pi laughed inwardly. At daybreak, a dense fog spread so thickly that nothing could be seen even directly ahead. Presently a wind arose; the fog dispersed and the clouds withdrew, revealing an unbroken line of fortified towns all along the southern bank. Spears and blades flashed in the sunlight atop their towers, while banners and streamers covered the walls. Within moments, several messengers came in succession to report, “From Nanxu along the river all the way to Stone City, for hundreds of li without a break, walls, ships, and carts stretch endlessly—all completed in a single night.” Cao Pi was greatly alarmed. In fact, Xu Sheng had bound reeds into human figures, dressed them all in blue, placed banners in their hands, and stationed them atop sham walls and counterfeit towers. Seeing so many men and horses upon the walls, how could the Wei soldiers fail to lose heart? Cao Pi sighed, “Though Wei has warriors by the thousand, there is nowhere to employ them. The men of Jiangnan are not to be conquered!”

p.src: While he was still marveling, a furious gale suddenly arose. White-crested waves towered to the sky, the river spray soaked the imperial robe, and the great vessel was on the verge of capsizing. In panic, Cao Zhen ordered Wen Ping to hasten over in a small boat and rescue the emperor. No one aboard the dragon barge could keep his footing. Wen Ping leaped aboard the dragon barge, carried Cao Pi on his back down into the small boat, and made for an inlet. Suddenly, an express rider came with a report: “Zhao Yun has led an army out of Yangping Pass and is advancing directly on Chang’an.” When Cao Pi heard this, his face changed with alarm, and he immediately ordered a retreat. The troops scattered and fled in every direction. The Wu troops came in pursuit from behind. Cao Pi issued an edict ordering them to abandon all imperial belongings and flee. Just as the dragon barge was about to enter the Huai, drums and horns suddenly sounded together and mighty battle cries shook the air, as a force charged in from the flank. The general at their head was none other than Sun Shao. The Wei troops could not withstand them; more than half were lost, and countless men drowned.

p.src: The generals fought with all their strength and rescued the ruler of Wei. After the ruler of Wei crossed the Huai River and had traveled less than thirty li, a belt of reeds in the river, which had been soaked beforehand with fish oil, was set ablaze throughout. The flames swept downstream before the wind, which blew with tremendous force. Flames filled the sky and cut off the dragon barge. Cao Pi was greatly alarmed and hurriedly transferred to a small boat. By the time he neared the bank, the dragon barge was already ablaze. Cao Pi hastily mounted a horse, but a force charged toward him along the bank, led by the general Ding Feng. Zhang Liao swiftly spurred forward to meet him, but Ding Feng struck him in the waist with an arrow. Xu Huang managed to rescue him, and together they protected the ruler of Wei as they fled. Countless troops were lost. Behind them, Sun Shao and Ding Feng seized horses, carriages and equipment, boats, weapons, and other matériel beyond count. The Wei army returned in utter defeat. Xu Sheng, the Wu general, received full credit for the great victory. The King of Wu rewarded him lavishly. After Zhang Liao returned to Xuchang, his arrow wound burst open, and he died. Cao Pi gave him a lavish burial, but that need not detain our tale.
